description: Assume a project has already failed, then work backward to find the causes and build prevention into the plan before the work begins.

steps.description: Define the project under review, its success criteria, and its timeline so the pre-mortem has a concrete target.

inputs.name: project-brief
inputs.desc: A short statement of what the project is meant to deliver.

inputs.name: success-criteria
inputs.desc: The measurable conditions that would mark the project as done.

outputs.name: project-frame
outputs.desc: A one paragraph definition of the project and its goal.

outputs.name: review-horizon
outputs.desc: The future date at which you will imagine the project has failed.

process: Write a one paragraph statement of what the project is meant to deliver and by when.
List the measurable success criteria that would mark the project as done.
Set the review horizon, the future date at which you will imagine the project has failed.

steps.description: Gather the people and viewpoints needed so the failure search covers the whole project, not one function.

inputs.name: project-frame
inputs.desc: The project definition from the framing step.

inputs.name: review-horizon
inputs.desc: The future failure date the group will reason from.

outputs.name: participant-list
outputs.desc: The people taking part in the pre-mortem.

outputs.name: viewpoint-map
outputs.desc: Which part of the project each participant sees most clearly.

process: Invite people who touch different parts of the project, including at least one skeptic.
Map each participant to the part of the project they see most clearly.
Confirm every major area has at least one person who can speak to its risks.

steps.description: State plainly that the project has already failed, then have each person privately write down every reason why.

inputs.name: participant-list
inputs.desc: The people taking part in the pre-mortem.

inputs.name: viewpoint-map
inputs.desc: Which part of the project each participant sees most clearly.

outputs.name: failure-statement
outputs.desc: The plain statement that the project has failed.

outputs.name: individual-reasons
outputs.desc: Each person's privately written reasons for the failure.

process: Read the failure statement aloud so the whole group accepts the project has failed.
Give each person silent time to write every reason the failure could have happened.
Collect the written reasons without discussion so no one anchors on another voice.

steps.description: Consolidate the written reasons into a single deduplicated list and group related causes together.

inputs.name: failure-statement
inputs.desc: The plain statement that the project has failed.

inputs.name: individual-reasons
inputs.desc: Each person's privately written reasons for the failure.

outputs.name: cause-list
outputs.desc: A single deduplicated list of failure causes.

outputs.name: cause-clusters
outputs.desc: Related causes grouped into named clusters.

process: Read every reason aloud and merge duplicates into one entry.
Group related causes into clusters such as scope, people, timing, and outside forces.
Name each cluster so the pattern behind the individual reasons is visible.

steps.description: Sort each cause along three axes: preventable or not, detectable early or not, and fatal or recoverable.

inputs.name: cause-list
inputs.desc: The deduplicated list of failure causes.

inputs.name: cause-clusters
inputs.desc: Related causes grouped into named clusters.

outputs.name: risk-categories
outputs.desc: Each cause marked preventable, detectable, and recoverable or not.

outputs.name: fatal-flags
outputs.desc: The causes that would be fatal rather than recoverable.

process: Mark whether each cause can be prevented by a change you control.
Mark whether each cause would show an early signal before it did damage.
Flag the causes that would be fatal to the project rather than recoverable.

steps.description: Rank the causes by likelihood and impact so attention goes to the few that matter most.

inputs.name: risk-categories
inputs.desc: Each cause marked preventable, detectable, and recoverable or not.

inputs.name: fatal-flags
inputs.desc: The causes that would be fatal rather than recoverable.

outputs.name: ranked-risks
outputs.desc: Causes ordered by combined likelihood and impact.

outputs.name: top-threats
outputs.desc: The handful of causes that most endanger the project.

process: Estimate the rough likelihood of each cause on a shared scale.
Estimate the impact of each cause if it occurred.
Order the causes by combined likelihood and impact and name the top threats.

steps.description: Design a specific prevention action for each top threat and fold it back into the project plan.

inputs.name: ranked-risks
inputs.desc: Causes ordered by combined likelihood and impact.

inputs.name: top-threats
inputs.desc: The handful of causes that most endanger the project.

outputs.name: prevention-actions
outputs.desc: One owned action per top threat that removes or reduces it.

outputs.name: plan-revisions
outputs.desc: The parts of the plan rewritten to include the actions.

process: For each top threat, write one action that removes or reduces the cause.
Assign an owner and a due date to every prevention action.
Rewrite the affected parts of the project plan to include the actions.

steps.description: Define the early warning signals that say a risk is becoming real and name who watches each one.

inputs.name: prevention-actions
inputs.desc: One owned action per top threat that removes or reduces it.

inputs.name: plan-revisions
inputs.desc: The parts of the plan rewritten to include the actions.

outputs.name: tripwire-signals
outputs.desc: The observable signals that a risk is starting to happen.

outputs.name: monitoring-plan
outputs.desc: Each signal with its owner and the response to it.

process: For each detectable risk, name the observable signal that it is starting to happen.
Assign one person to watch each signal and state how often they check it.
Write the monitoring plan that lists every signal, its owner, and the response.

description: Solve a problem by inverting it: instead of asking how to succeed, list every way to guarantee failure, then remove those paths from the plan.

steps.description: Define the problem and the outcome you want in plain terms before you flip it.

inputs.name: problem-statement
inputs.desc: The problem you are trying to solve.

inputs.name: desired-outcome
inputs.desc: The result you want to reach.

outputs.name: goal-definition
outputs.desc: The goal written as a single clear sentence.

outputs.name: success-markers
outputs.desc: The signs that would tell you the outcome was reached.

process: Write the problem as a single sentence that names what you are trying to achieve.
List the markers that would tell you the outcome was reached.
Set aside any proposed solution so the inversion starts from the goal, not a plan.

steps.description: Restate the goal as its opposite: how would you guarantee this fails?

inputs.name: goal-definition
inputs.desc: The goal written as a single clear sentence.

inputs.name: success-markers
inputs.desc: The signs that would tell you the outcome was reached.

outputs.name: failure-question
outputs.desc: The goal rewritten as a question about causing failure.

outputs.name: failure-frame
outputs.desc: The failure stated as something you are trying to produce.

process: Rewrite the goal as a question about causing the worst result.
Confirm the failure question is the true inverse of the stated goal.
Frame the failure as something you are actively trying to produce.

steps.description: Enumerate every way the effort could fail, holding back no path as too unlikely.

inputs.name: failure-question
inputs.desc: The goal rewritten as a question about causing failure.

inputs.name: failure-frame
inputs.desc: The failure stated as something you are trying to produce.

outputs.name: failure-paths
outputs.desc: Every action or condition that would move toward failure.

outputs.name: failure-ranked
outputs.desc: The failure paths ordered by how easily each could happen.

process: Brainstorm every action or condition that would move toward failure.
Include slow failures and sudden ones, inside causes and outside causes.
Rank the failure paths by how easily each could happen.

steps.description: Hold the current plan against each failure path and mark where the plan already invites that failure.

inputs.name: failure-paths
inputs.desc: Every action or condition that would move toward failure.

inputs.name: failure-ranked
inputs.desc: The failure paths ordered by how easily each could happen.

outputs.name: plan-exposure
outputs.desc: Where the current plan does nothing to stop a failure path.

outputs.name: vulnerable-points
outputs.desc: The points where the plan actively moves toward failure.

process: Walk the current plan step by step against each ranked failure path.
Mark every place where the plan does nothing to stop a failure path.
Record the points where the plan actively moves toward a failure path.

steps.description: Summarize where the plan is most exposed and which gaps deserve attention first.

inputs.name: plan-exposure
inputs.desc: Where the current plan does nothing to stop a failure path.

inputs.name: vulnerable-points
inputs.desc: The points where the plan actively moves toward failure.

outputs.name: exposure-summary
outputs.desc: Vulnerable points grouped by the part of the plan they sit in.

outputs.name: priority-gaps
outputs.desc: The gaps that would sink the effort if left open.

process: Group the vulnerable points by the part of the plan they sit in.
Rate each gap by how directly it leads to failure.
Name the priority gaps that would sink the effort if left open.

steps.description: Redesign the plan so each priority failure path is removed or made far less likely.

inputs.name: exposure-summary
inputs.desc: Vulnerable points grouped by the part of the plan they sit in.

inputs.name: priority-gaps
inputs.desc: The gaps that would sink the effort if left open.

outputs.name: plan-changes
outputs.desc: The changes that close each priority failure path.

outputs.name: removed-modes
outputs.desc: The failure modes the changes take off the table.

process: For each priority gap, write a change that closes the failure path.
Prefer changes that remove a failure path outright over ones that only reduce it.
Record which failure modes the changes remove.

steps.description: Check the revised plan against the original failure list and record the risks that still remain.

inputs.name: plan-changes
inputs.desc: The changes that close each priority failure path.

inputs.name: removed-modes
inputs.desc: The failure modes the changes take off the table.

outputs.name: revised-plan
outputs.desc: The plan after the failure paths are closed.

outputs.name: residual-risks
outputs.desc: The risks the plan accepts on purpose.

process: Re-run the full failure list against the revised plan.
Confirm each priority failure path is now blocked or far less likely.
List the residual risks that the plan accepts on purpose.

description: For every decision ask 'and then what?' several times, mapping the first, second, and third order effects before you choose.

steps.description: Define the decision and name the obvious first thing that happens if you take it.

inputs.name: decision-statement
inputs.desc: The decision you are weighing.

inputs.name: decision-context
inputs.desc: The situation the decision sits in.

outputs.name: decision-defined
outputs.desc: The decision stated as a clear choice.

outputs.name: obvious-effect
outputs.desc: The immediate result most people would expect.

process: State the decision as a clear choice between taking an action and not taking it.
Write the immediate result that most people would expect.
Note why that immediate result looks attractive on its own.

steps.description: List the direct, near-term effects of the decision, the ones that follow right away.

inputs.name: decision-defined
inputs.desc: The decision stated as a clear choice.

inputs.name: obvious-effect
inputs.desc: The immediate result most people would expect.

outputs.name: first-order-effects
outputs.desc: The direct, near-term effects of the decision.

outputs.name: first-order-notes
outputs.desc: Which first-order effects are good and which are bad.

process: List every effect that follows directly from the action.
Keep these to near-term results that need no further chain of events.
Note which first-order effects are good and which are bad.

steps.description: Ask 'and then what?' once: for each first-order effect, name what it causes next.

inputs.name: first-order-effects
inputs.desc: The direct, near-term effects of the decision.

inputs.name: first-order-notes
inputs.desc: Which first-order effects are good and which are bad.

outputs.name: second-order-effects
outputs.desc: What each first-order effect sets off in turn.

outputs.name: second-order-notes
outputs.desc: Where a good first-order effect starts to turn bad.

process: For each first-order effect, ask what it leads to in turn.
Write the second-order effects that each first-order effect sets off.
Note where a good first-order effect starts to turn bad.

steps.description: Ask 'and then what?' again: trace the second-order effects out to their third-order results.

inputs.name: second-order-effects
inputs.desc: What each first-order effect sets off in turn.

inputs.name: second-order-notes
inputs.desc: Where a good first-order effect starts to turn bad.

outputs.name: third-order-effects
outputs.desc: The effects at the end of each chain.

outputs.name: order-chain
outputs.desc: The full chain from decision to third-order result.

process: For each second-order effect, ask what it leads to over a longer span.
Write the third-order effects at the end of each chain.
Assemble the full chain from decision to third-order result.

steps.description: Assign a rough probability to each branch so unlikely chains do not carry equal weight.

inputs.name: third-order-effects
inputs.desc: The effects at the end of each chain.

inputs.name: order-chain
inputs.desc: The full chain from decision to third-order result.

outputs.name: weighted-effects
outputs.desc: Each branch carrying the odds of reaching it.

outputs.name: likely-branches
outputs.desc: The branches that are both likely and heavy in effect.

process: Give each branch of effects a rough probability on a shared scale.
Multiply along each chain so later effects carry the odds of getting there.
Mark the branches that are both likely and heavy in effect.

steps.description: Net the orders together and surface cases where a first-order good hides a third-order harm.

inputs.name: weighted-effects
inputs.desc: Each branch carrying the odds of reaching it.

inputs.name: likely-branches
inputs.desc: The branches that are both likely and heavy in effect.

outputs.name: net-score
outputs.desc: The weighted good and bad effects summed across all orders.

outputs.name: hidden-costs
outputs.desc: The costs that only appear past the first order.

process: Add the weighted good and bad effects across all orders for each option.
Flag any option whose first-order looks good but whose later orders are bad.
Record the hidden costs that only appear past the first order.

steps.description: Make the call using the full map of effects rather than the first-order result alone.

inputs.name: net-score
inputs.desc: The weighted good and bad effects summed across all orders.

inputs.name: hidden-costs
inputs.desc: The costs that only appear past the first order.

outputs.name: decision-call
outputs.desc: The option chosen with later orders in view.

outputs.name: decision-rationale
outputs.desc: The chain of effects behind the call, on record.

process: Compare the options by their net score across all orders.
Choose the option whose later-order effects you are willing to live with.
Write the rationale so the chain of effects behind the call is on record.

description: Classify decisions as one-way doors that deserve deep analysis or two-way doors you can decide fast, so you stop treating every choice as irreversible.

steps.description: Gather the decisions waiting to be made so each can be filtered by how reversible it is.

inputs.name: decision-owner
inputs.desc: Who is accountable for the decisions.

outputs.name: pending-decisions
outputs.desc: The listed decisions with what each commits you to.

outputs.name: decision-notes
outputs.desc: Which decisions are blocking other work.

process: List every decision currently waiting to be made.
Write one line on what each decision commits you to.
Note which decisions are blocking other work.

steps.description: For each decision, test whether it is a one-way door or a two-way door you can walk back through.

inputs.name: pending-decisions
inputs.desc: The listed decisions with what each commits you to.

inputs.name: decision-notes
inputs.desc: Which decisions are blocking other work.

outputs.name: door-test-results

outputs.name: undo-cost

process: Ask for each decision whether you could reverse it later and at what cost.
Record the cost and time it would take to undo each decision.
Separate decisions you could unwind from those you could not.

steps.description: Label each decision Type 1, irreversible and high stakes, or Type 2, reversible and low stakes.

inputs.name: door-test-results
inputs.desc: Whether each decision can be reversed later.

inputs.name: undo-cost
inputs.desc: The cost and time to undo each decision.

outputs.name: type-labels

outputs.name: classification-notes
outputs.desc: Why each decision earned its label.

process: Label a decision Type 1 when reversing it would be very costly or impossible.
Label a decision Type 2 when it can be reversed at low cost.
Write why each decision earned its label.

steps.description: Route Type 1 decisions to deep analysis and Type 2 decisions to a fast decide-and-adjust path.

inputs.name: type-labels
inputs.desc: Each decision labeled Type 1 or Type 2.

inputs.name: classification-notes
inputs.desc: Why each decision earned its label.

outputs.name: routing-plan
outputs.desc: Which path each decision takes based on its type.

outputs.name: analysis-depth
outputs.desc: How much analysis each path gets.

process: Send each Type 1 decision to a slower path with more review.
Send each Type 2 decision to a fast path with a quick owner and deadline.
Set how much analysis each path gets so effort matches stakes.

steps.description: Catch the common error of treating a reversible decision as if it were irreversible.

inputs.name: routing-plan
inputs.desc: Which path each decision takes based on its type.

inputs.name: analysis-depth
inputs.desc: How much analysis each path gets.

outputs.name: corrected-labels
outputs.desc: Over-labeled decisions moved to the fast path.

outputs.name: speed-gains
outputs.desc: The time saved by not over-analyzing reversible choices.

process: Review the Type 1 pile for decisions that are actually reversible.
Move any over-labeled decision to the Type 2 fast path.
Record the time saved by not over-analyzing reversible choices.

steps.description: Assign a timeline and owner to each decision so the pace matches its type.

inputs.name: corrected-labels
inputs.desc: Over-labeled decisions moved to the fast path.

inputs.name: speed-gains
inputs.desc: The time saved by not over-analyzing reversible choices.

outputs.name: decision-schedule

outputs.name: speed-rules

process: Set a deadline for each decision that fits its type.
